key_facts: **Wayve가 Mercedes-Benz와 상용 파트너십을 체결**, 자동화 주행 기술을 최소 한 개 모델에 통합해 향후 2년 내 배치 예정
해당 기술은 **Level 2 등급**으로, 특정 주행 조작을 수행하지만 운전자가 계속 개입해야 함
이는 완전자율(Level 4) 제품이 아니며, Nissan·Stellantis와의 유사한 계약에 이어진 것
이러한 파트너십들은 Wayve의 완전자율주행 제품으로도 문을 열어, 올해 초 Nissan·Uber와 함께 도쿄 로보택시 서비스 출시 파트너십을 발표한 바 있음
summary_data.why_matters: 완성차 업체와의 Level 2 상용 파트너십은 Wayve에게 대규모 차량 보급을 통한 데이터·매출 확보 경로를 제공하며, 이는 완전자율주행(Level 4) 로보택시 사업 확장의 기반이 된다. **AV 업계가 파트너십 기반 확장, 지역 집중형 확장(Waymo), 트럭 중심 확장(Aurora) 등 서로 다른 스케일링 전략을 택하는 흐름 속에서 Wayve는 파트너십 중심 전략의 대표 사례로 부각**된다.
summary_data.subject_angle: **Wayve는 Level 2 ADAS 공급을 통해 완성차 업체들의 광범위한 차량 플랫폼에 접근하며, 이를 완전자율(Level 4) 로보택시 사업(Tokyo, Nissan·Uber 협력)으로 이어지는 단계적 확장 경로로 활용**하고 있다.
summary_data.focus_angle: **사업·상용화 관점에서 Wayve의 Mercedes-Benz 딜은 아직 Rumor를 넘어 Announced 단계이며, 상용화는 향후 2년 내 최소 1개 모델·Level 2 등급으로 제한적**이다. 고객·지역 범위는 Mercedes-Benz 특정 모델(구체적 차종·지역 미확인)에 한정되어 있으나, Nissan·Stellantis 파트너십과 함께 Wayve의 완성차 OEM 다변화 전략 및 Level 4 로보택시(Tokyo) 확장의 기반으로 기능한다.

cards.body: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility! Autonomous vehicle technology is not yet ubiquitous or mainstream. Readers here might shout, “It’s everywhere!” but I can tell you that it is not — although I understand why folks in the San Francisco Bay Area might disagree. The tech is, however, being commercialized and that transition from testing to commercial product has me thinking about scale. A few strategies are emerging. Scale through partnerships. A couple of announcements this week highlighted this strategy. Wayve locked in a commercial partnership with Mercedes-Benz to integrate the startup’s automated driving tech into at least one model set to be deployed within the next two years. This is a Level 2 type product, meaning it handles certain driving maneuvers but still requires the human driver to remain engaged. While this is not a Level 4, or fully driverless product, it gives Wayve reach and follows similar deals with Nissan and Stellantis. Those partnerships have also opened doors for its fully driverless product. Earlier this year, Wayve announced a partnership with Nissan and Uber to launch a robotaxi service in Tokyo. Widespread and concentrated, all at once. As I wrote this week, Waymo’s commercial robotaxi ramp-up looks expansive, both in geographic reach and ridership. And by almost every measure, it is — until you pay attention to where the bulk of those robotaxis are actually showing up. I looked at vehicle registration data and found that, at least for now, Waymo is concentrating its efforts in just two states. About 80% of Waymo’s roughly 4,000 robotaxis are in California and Texas, and Texas is where the action is now: Waymo’s fleet there has grown by more than 49% in the past three weeks. Waymo is also scaling by seeking out new kinds of users: teenagers. I might put Aurora, a company developing and commercializing self-driving trucks, somewhere between these two categories. Aurora is clearly focused on Texas, but it has cast a wide net when it comes to partners. CEO Chris Urmson is also clearly bullish on how the company will scale over the next four years, noting this week that Aurora has “emerged from the building stage.” The company said it’s targeting more than 30,000 driverless trucks in operation by 2030. The company plans to have more than 200 driverless trucks by the end of the year. A little bird Our little bird items are typically just that: small yet notable nuggets of insider information from across the transportation industry. But every now and then, a tip turns into something much bigger. That’s what happened a few weeks ago, when Zoox workers reached out to senior reporter Sean O’Kane about a problem with the company’s test fleet in Atlanta.
